name: Mojo 0.6.0 multi-threaded GEMM in dev0x13/gemm-benchmark-2023
baseline: Eigen 3.4.0 (C++, clang++ -O3 -march=native -fopenmp); also OpenBLAS 0.3.25 and Intel MKL called from C++ and a naive C++ triple loop, all built with clang++ -O3 -march=native
workload: Single-precision (DType.float32) GEMM, 19 problem shapes from 128x128x128 to 1024x2560x1024, GFLOPS, multi-threaded and single-threaded tables; the Mojo code is src/matmul.mojo run with 'mojo matmul.mojo'.
claimed_speedup: No speedup is claimed by the README; the reference tables give GFLOPS. Multi-thread, Mojo ('Swizzled') vs Eigen: 256x1024x4096 835.4 vs 378.8 (2.2x, derived from page data), 256x4096x1024 818.0 vs 428.0 (1.9x), 1024x2560x1024 808.8 vs 437.3 (1.8x), 128x768x3072 814.3 vs 381.2 (2.1x). Versus OpenBLAS the result is mixed: 256x4096x1024 818.0 vs 770.9 and 128x4096x1024 795.0 vs 688.9 (Mojo ahead), 256x1024x4096 835.4 vs 860.6 and 1024x2560x1024 808.8 vs 1126.2 (OpenBLAS ahead). MKL is ahead on every shape (for example 1063.6 vs 835.4 GFLOPS). Mojo loses on small shapes (128x128x128: 24.4 vs Eigen 109.0 vs OpenBLAS 143.6) and the single-thread Mojo ('Vectorized') column is far behind Eigen (10.0 vs 56.0 on 256x1024x4096) and about level with the naive C++ loop (11.0).
compiler_and_flags: C++ baselines: clang++ -O3 -march=native (src/Makefile; -fopenmp for Eigen and OpenBLAS, MKL linked with libiomp5), Ubuntu 22.04 Docker image; single-thread runs set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1. Mojo 0.6.0 via 'mojo matmul.mojo' (no optimization flags given).
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (README says 16 cores; AWS EC2 c5.4xlarge), Ubuntu 22.04
tradeoffs: Mojo 0.6.0 (December 2023) is an early release and the language and its APIs have changed since; installing it needs a Modular auth token. The kernel is float32 only and assumes tile-friendly shapes.
caveats: Numbers come from one machine and one run per cell with no spread reported. Both Mojo tables show 0.0 GFLOPS for 1024x352x512 with no explanation. The README lists MKL 2020.4.304 while the Dockerfile ARG pins MKL 2024.0.0.49673, so the MKL version actually used is unclear. The win over Eigen is partly an Eigen scaling issue (Eigen goes from about 57 GFLOPS single-thread to about 380-440 multi-thread on 16 vCPUs). The README does not claim Mojo is faster, it only publishes the table; this is a reading of that table. The Mojo kernel is Modular's matmul.mojo sample (Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions header) placed in an MIT repo. Mojo is not faster than OpenBLAS or MKL overall.
found_via: WebSearch 'Mojo faster than C++ benchmark github -O3 clang matmul' surfaced dev0x13/gemm-benchmark-2023; opened the repo page, README, Dockerfile, src/Makefile, src/run_benchmark.sh, src/matmul.mojo and the commits page
why_faster: No mechanism in the README. The Mojo sample code (src/matmul.mojo comments) applies SIMD vectorize, parallelize across rows, 2D tiling and a swizzled tile order to a naive matmul; Eigen and OpenBLAS use their own packed GEMM kernels, so the algorithms differ.

name: Yao.jl (Julia quantum circuit simulator) in Roger-luo/quantum-benchmarks
baseline: Qulacs 0.1.9 (C++ with Python bindings) and QuEST via pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 (C library behind a Python wrapper), single-thread full-amplitude state-vector simulation
workload: Time per gate for X, H, CNOT and T gates on 4 to 25 qubits, and time for a parameterized circuit on 4 to 25 qubits, single thread, Yao v0.6.1 against qulacs, QuEST, qiskit-aer, ProjectQ, Cirq and PennyLane.
claimed_speedup: Read off the repo's 'relative to Yao' chart images (approximate, no tables published). At 25 qubits: parameterized circuit, qulacs about 1.9x and QuEST about 8x slower than Yao; single gates, QuEST about 2.4x slower on X, 1.8x on H, 2.5x on CNOT, but about 0.75 (QuEST faster) on T; qulacs roughly equal to Yao on X, CNOT and T and about 0.6 of Yao's time (faster) on H. Below about 10 qubits qulacs is faster than Yao (about 0.34x of Yao's time at 4 qubits in the parameterized circuit).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.3.0 (LLVM 6.0.1 ORCJIT, skylake), BLAS Intel MKL, Python 3.7.3; compile flags of the Qulacs and QuEST builds are not stated (installed by the repo's bin/benchmark install script).
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz (single thread); Tesla V100 for the CUDA rows
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars (Yao.jl); the benchmark repo has 129 stars
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and compilation time is not part of the per-gate timings. Qulacs is faster on small circuits and the advantage of Yao appears only at 20 or more qubits.
caveats: The benchmark repo is written by Yao's author (reviewed by maintainers of several competitors per its acknowledgements), so it is first-party. Results are marked 'only up to date till 2020' and the benchmark repo's last commit is 2022-05-17; package versions are old (qulacs 0.1.9, Julia 1.3.0). RESULTS.md and the README give only chart images, so every ratio here is read off a log-scale chart. QuEST is driven through pyquest-cffi, so Python wrapper overhead may be inside its timings. The README says 'mean estimator' timings for DDSIM only. The baseline is not a C or C++ program at a stated -O3.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/Roger-luo/quantum-benchmarks (found while checking Julia packages with C or C++ competitors); opened README, RESULTS.md, images/gates_relative.png and images/pcircuit_relative.png

name: Julia Base sort! in LilithHafner/InterLanguageSortingComparisons
baseline: C++ std::sort on std::vector<double> (src/script.cpp, Apple clang 13 under the g++ name) and C qsort with a comparator callback (src/script.c), same suite
workload: Sorting-dominated workload: fill a vector of 3^i uniform random Float64 values, sort it, compute a dot product; the sorting time is inferred by subtracting a no-sort control run; ns per element for 3 to 3^15 elements.
claimed_speedup: data.txt at 3^14 = 4,782,969 elements, ns per element of sorting: Julia 1.9.0-beta3 35.1, Julia 1.8.5 92.5, C++ 207.6, C gcc 307.2, so Julia 1.9 is 5.9x and Julia 1.8 2.2x faster than C++ (derived from page data). README: 'Julia and Rust outperform other languages'.
compiler_and_flags: Commands recorded in data.txt: C 'gcc script.c', C++ 'g++ -std=c++11 script.cpp' (Apple LLVM 13.0.0 / clang-1300.0.27.3) with no -O flag, so the C and C++ baselines are unoptimized; Julia 1.9.0-beta3 and 1.8.5; Rust 'cargo run --release'.
hardware: 2019 MacBook Air, 1.6 GHz dual-core Intel Core i5, 8 GB
tradeoffs: Algorithm difference: the AcceleratedKernels.jl README calls Julia's Base CPU sort a radix sort, unlike std::sort's introsort and the C qsort comparator version; Julia JIT warm-up is not in the per-element numbers.
caveats: The C and C++ programs were compiled without any optimization flag (-O0 equivalent per the commands in data.txt), which probably makes much of the 5.9x and 8.8x figures an unoptimized-baseline artifact; the Julia rows were not matched against -O3 C++. The C row is qsort with a function-pointer comparator, a different algorithm from std::sort. Each data point is a single trial (README says so). The C++ rows are not control-subtracted: script.cpp multiplies the total time by a fixed 0.85 (the comment says 0.8, the label prints 80%) because subtraction sometimes went negative. No LICENSE file was found (raw LICENSE request returned 404), so the code is reference only. A sorting-heavy workload rather than numerics proper, kept here because it is an array-processing comparison.
found_via: GitHub: README of JuliaGPU/AcceleratedKernels.jl links this repo ('already one of the fastest' Julia radix sort); opened README, figure.png, data.txt, src/script.cpp, src/script.c, src/script.jl and the commits page
why_faster: Not stated for C++; the README only says the benchmark isolates sorting speed. Julia's Base sort uses a different (radix-based) algorithm for Float64 at these sizes, inferred from the AcceleratedKernels README calling it a radix sort.

name: Julia (@fastmath loop) in anicusan/AcceleratedKernels-Benchmark: Lennard-Jones-Gauss kernel
baseline: C version of the same kernel (arithmetic_kernel.c, ljg_cpu with powf) called from Julia via ccall, built with the repo Makefile at -O2; plus a C variant with hand-written integer powers (ljg_cpu2) and a C OpenMP variant
workload: Lennard-Jones-Gauss potential on single-precision (Float32) atom position arrays of N = 100,000,000 points (potential_kernel.jl), one thread for 'CPU Base' (the ljg_cpu! function) and C, timings in ms (median with spread) on Apple M3 Max and Intel 8360Y; a radial basis function kernel is in the same table.
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.csv medians (ms): LJG Apple M3 Max, Julia Base 219.47 vs C 1253.0 (5.7x, derived from page data) vs C with hand-written powf 426.37 (1.9x, derived); LJG Intel 8360Y, Julia Base 335.80 vs C 470.61 (1.4x, derived) vs hand-written 381.33 (1.1x, derived). The RBF kernel goes the other way: C 210.57 vs Julia Base 318.35 on M3 Max and C 641.26 vs Julia 734.22 on Intel. AcceleratedKernels.jl on CPU against C OpenMP is parity: LJG 27.93 vs 28.53 (M3 Max), 49.46 vs 53.01 (Intel).
compiler_and_flags: C: Makefile FLAGS = -Wall -Werror -Wextra -fPIC -lm -O2 using $(CC) (compiler not named; '-Xclang -fopenmp' with Homebrew libomp suggests Apple clang), no -O3, -march=native or -ffast-math. Julia: ljg_cpu! (the 'CPU Base' row) in potential_kernel.jl uses '@inbounds @fastmath'; Julia version not stated in the files opened.
hardware: Apple M3 Max (aarch64) and Intel 8360Y (x86_64); GPUs for the AcceleratedKernels rows
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (benchmark repo); the library JuliaGPU/AcceleratedKernels.jl has 203 stars
tradeoffs: Benchmark repo accompanies the AcceleratedKernels.jl paper; the Julia kernel code is not a reusable library.
caveats: Not like for like: the C code is built at -O2 without fast-math and calls libm powf for every power, while the Julia loop is compiled with @fastmath, and Julia lowers powers with literal integer exponents to multiplications while @fastmath lets LLVM reassociate and vectorize (my inference, not stated by the repo); the repo's own 'C (hand-written powf)' row narrows the gap to 1.1x on Intel. Julia loses on the RBF kernel. The repo has no README and states no claim that Julia beats C; the numbers are a table of results for a paper. Results are also in an image and Benchmark.xlsx. The 'CPU Base' benchmark label in potential_kernel.jl is the ljg_cpu! function, matching the table's 'Julia Base' row.
found_via: GitHub: README of JuliaGPU/AcceleratedKernels.jl links this benchmark repo; opened the repo page, ArithmeticBenchmark/Makefile, arithmetic_kernel.c, potential_kernel.jl, benchmarks.csv and ArithmeticBenchmarkTable.png
why_faster: Not stated by the source. Inferred from the code: @fastmath plus literal integer powers (lowered to multiplications) in Julia versus libm powf at -O2 without fast-math in C.
